body: Investing in information systems simply because they are a necessity of doing business describes which strategic business objective?

options.hint: Correct. When IS are needed just to stay in business (e.g. ATMs in banking, regulatory reporting), the objective is survival.
Operational excellence is about efficiency and productivity, not necessity.
That objective is about knowing and serving customers and suppliers better.
That objective is about better information for managers' decisions.

hint: Which objective is about staying in business at all?
explanation: Laudon & Laudon list six strategic objectives for investing in IS. Survival covers investments made because they are necessities of doing business — driven by industry change (every bank needing ATMs) or by law and regulation.

body: Doing things better than competitors, charging less for superior products and responding to customers and suppliers in real time all add up to which business objective?

options.hint: Operational excellence is one ingredient, but the combined result described here is wider.

options.text: New products, services and business models
options.hint: This is about creating new offerings, not out-performing rivals.
Correct. Achieving the other objectives together usually yields a competitive advantage — higher sales and profits rivals cannot match.
Survival is investment out of necessity.

hint: The question describes beating rivals. Which objective is about that?
explanation: When firms achieve operational excellence, new products and business models, customer/supplier intimacy and improved decision making, they have usually achieved a competitive advantage.

body: Giving managers real-time data from the marketplace so they no longer rely on forecasts, best guesses and luck supports which business objective?

options.hint: That is about efficiency of operations.
Correct. Right information at the right time lets managers make informed decisions.
That is about serving customers better.
Survival is investment out of necessity.

hint: Who uses real-time data, and for what?
explanation: Improved decision making: IS let managers use real-time data from the marketplace instead of forecasts and guesses, reducing poor decisions that raise costs and lose customers.

body: Engineers, scientists and architects who design products or services and create new knowledge for the firm are classified as:

options.hint: Data workers (secretaries, clerks) process paperwork rather than create knowledge.
These workers actually produce the product or deliver the service.
Correct. Knowledge workers create new knowledge and design products or services.
Middle managers carry out the programs and plans of senior management.

hint: Their main output is new knowledge.
explanation: Knowledge workers — engineers, scientists, architects — design products or services and create new knowledge for the firm. They are supported by knowledge work systems.

body: The three principal levels of management within a business hierarchy are:

options.hint: These are not the standard three levels.

options.text: Senior management, middle management and operational management
options.hint: Correct. Senior management makes long-range strategic decisions, middle management carries out plans, operational management monitors daily activities.

options.text: Board of directors, CEO and staff
options.hint: This mixes governance with roles.
Technical staff is not a management level.

hint: Think of the management pyramid from top to bottom.
explanation: A business hierarchy has three principal management levels: senior (strategic), middle (tactical) and operational management, supported by knowledge workers, data workers and production or service workers.

body: Which tool displays, on a single screen, graphs and charts of key performance indicators for managing a company?

options.hint: Correct. A digital dashboard shows KPIs on one screen and is typical of executive support systems.
A TPS records routine transactions; it does not present KPIs.
A data warehouse stores data for analysis; it is not a display tool.
A spreadsheet can chart data, but this term is for an executive KPI screen.

hint: Think of a car's instrument panel for managers.
explanation: A digital dashboard displays on a single screen graphs and charts of key performance indicators. It is the typical front end of an executive support system.

body: In the business perspective on information systems, raw data that is systematically acquired and transformed through stages that each add value to the information is called:

options.hint: Correct. Each stage — acquiring, transforming, distributing — adds value that supports decisions and raises profitability.
The value chain model is Porter's model of a firm's primary and support activities.
BPR is the radical redesign of business processes.
The SDLC is how systems are built.

hint: It is a 'chain' through which information gains value.
explanation: From a business perspective, an information system is part of a series of value-adding activities — the information value chain — in which raw data is acquired and transformed to improve decisions, firm performance and profitability.

body: Which level of management is responsible for monitoring the daily activities of the business?

options.hint: Senior management makes long-range strategic decisions.
Middle management carries out programs and plans of senior management.
Knowledge workers are not a management level.
Correct. Operational managers monitor the firm's daily activities.

hint: Who supervises day-to-day work?
explanation: Operational management is responsible for monitoring the daily activities of the business, and is mainly served by transaction processing systems.

body: The shared technology resources — hardware, software, data management and networking — that provide the platform for a firm's specific information system applications are called:

options.hint: IS literacy is broad knowledge of IS, not a set of resources.
Complementary assets are organizational and managerial investments that help IT produce value.
Correct. IT infrastructure is the shared platform on which a firm's applications run.
The information value chain describes how data gains value.

hint: It is the 'foundation' the specific systems are built on.
explanation: IT infrastructure — computer hardware, software, data management technology, and networking and telecommunications technology, plus the people to run them — provides the platform on which a firm builds its specific information systems.

body: Which of the following includes the physical devices and software that link various pieces of hardware and transfer data from one physical location to another?

options.hint: That covers the computers and programs themselves, not linking them.
That organizes and stores data.
VoIP is one service, not the category.
Correct. It links hardware and moves data between locations.

hint: Which technology connects things?
explanation: Networking and telecommunications technology consists of physical devices and software that link pieces of hardware and transfer data between locations — one of the four parts of IT infrastructure.

body: Precise rules, procedures and practices that an organization develops to cope with virtually all expected situations are called:

options.hint: A business model describes how a firm makes money.
Culture is the set of unquestioned assumptions behind an organization.
Correct. Routines (standard operating procedures) are precise rules and practices for expected situations.
Best practices are the most successful methods found across an industry.

hint: These are also called standard operating procedures.
explanation: Routines — also called standard operating procedures — are precise rules, procedures and practices developed to cope with virtually all expected situations. Business processes are collections of routines.

body: According to transaction cost theory, firms and nations seek to economize on which costs incurred when buying in the marketplace what they cannot make themselves?

options.hint: Agency costs come from supervising and managing employees (agency theory).
Correct. IT lowers transaction costs, so firms can shrink and buy more from outside.
Switching costs are what customers pay to change supplier.
Opportunity cost is the value of the next best alternative.

hint: The theory is named after the cost.
explanation: Transaction cost theory: firms economize on transaction costs — the costs of buying in the market (locating suppliers, negotiating contracts, monitoring them). IT reduces these costs, so firms can outsource more and grow revenue without growing in size.

body: According to agency theory, the firm is viewed as a:

options.hint: That is the microeconomic view, not agency theory.

options.text: Task force organization that must respond to rapidly changing environments
options.hint: That describes an adhocracy.
That describes an organizational structure, not the theory.
Correct. Agents (employees) need supervision because they pursue their own interests.

hint: Agency theory is about principals hiring agents who may not act in the owner's interest.
explanation: Agency theory views the firm as a 'nexus of contracts' among self-interested individuals rather than a unified profit-maximizing entity. Supervising agents creates agency costs, which IT can reduce, allowing flatter organizations.

body: The four major competitive strategies that firms can use, often enabled by IT, are:

options.text: Low-cost leadership; new market entrants; product differentiation; focus on market niche
options.hint: New market entrants is one of Porter's forces, not a strategy.

options.text: Low-cost leadership; product differentiation; focus on market niche; and customer and supplier intimacy
options.hint: Correct. These are the four generic IT-enabled strategies for dealing with competitive forces.

options.text: Operational excellence; survival; competitive advantage; improved decision making
options.hint: These are strategic business objectives of investing in IS.
These are Porter's competitive forces.

hint: Strategies are what a firm does; forces are what it faces.
explanation: The four generic strategies: low-cost leadership, product differentiation, focus on market niche, and strengthening customer and supplier intimacy.

body: Which model is used to describe the interaction of external influences — threats and opportunities — that affect an organization's strategy and ability to compete?

options.hint: Network economics is about the value of adding participants to a network.
Correct. Porter's competitive forces model looks at competitors, new entrants, substitutes, customers and suppliers.
The value chain looks inward at the firm's activities.
Transaction cost theory explains firm size.

hint: Porter's model of five external forces.
explanation: Porter's competitive forces model describes the external influences — traditional competitors, new market entrants, substitute products, customers and suppliers — that shape a firm's strategy.

body: Which information systems capability best supports a strategy of focusing on a market niche?

options.hint: These mainly support low-cost leadership or supplier intimacy.
These mainly support low-cost leadership.
Mass customization supports product differentiation.
Correct. Analysing customer data lets a firm identify and serve a narrow target market better than rivals.

hint: To serve a narrow market, you need to know exactly who is in it.
explanation: Focus on market niche relies on IS that produce and analyse data for finely tuned sales and marketing — data mining and intensive customer data analysis (e.g. Hilton's OnQ identifying its most profitable guests).

body: The Internet raises the bargaining power of customers by:

options.text: Creating new opportunities for building loyal customer bases
options.hint: That would reduce customer power.

options.text: Making the benefits of using technology available to everyone
options.hint: Close, but it is information, not technology benefits, that shifts power.
Correct. With prices and product information easy to compare, customers can switch easily.
Lower transaction costs mainly affect firms.

hint: What can customers now see that they could not before?
explanation: The Internet makes information about prices, products and suppliers available to everyone, so customers can compare and switch easily — raising their bargaining power.

body: The primary activities of a firm's value chain are:

options.text: Inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, sales and marketing, and service
options.hint: Correct. These are directly related to producing and distributing the firm's products.

options.text: Administration and management, human resources, technology and procurement
options.hint: These are support activities.
Procurement is a support activity, and logistics is missing.

options.text: Planning, analysis, design, implementation and maintenance
options.hint: These are SDLC phases.

hint: Primary activities follow the product from raw materials to after-sales.
explanation: In Porter's value chain, primary activities are directly related to production and distribution: inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, sales and marketing, and service. Support activities (administration, HR, technology, procurement) make them possible.

body: The most successful solutions or problem-solving methods that have been developed by a specific organization or industry for consistently achieving a business objective are called:

options.hint: A core competency is an activity a firm is world-class at.
Benchmarking compares a firm against standards; it is not the method itself.
Routines are a firm's standard operating procedures.
Correct. Best practices are the most successful methods found for achieving a business objective.

hint: They are the 'best' way known to do something.
explanation: Best practices are the most successful solutions or problem-solving methods developed by a specific organization or industry. Firms compare themselves against them through benchmarking.

body: In network economics, the economic model of a network:

options.text: Is based on the law of diminishing returns
options.hint: That is traditional economics; networks show increasing returns.

options.text: Sees the cost of adding new members as a barrier
options.hint: Adding members is nearly free.

options.text: Sees the cost of adding new members as inconsequential
options.hint: Correct. The marginal cost of adding a participant is about zero while the value to all members grows.
It applies especially to digital networks.

hint: What does it cost to add one more user to a digital network?
explanation: Network economics: the cost of adding another participant is close to zero, while the marginal gain — more value for everyone on the network — can be much larger. This is why IT-based networks (like the Internet or a marketplace) become more valuable as they grow.

body:
Cyberwarfare — attacks by states and organised groups on a nation's computer systems and critical infrastructure.

State any five reasons for or against why cyberwarfare is a serious problem.
answer:
Cyberwarfare poses a unique and daunting set of challenges — detecting and preventing intrusions, and tracking down perpetrators and bringing them to justice. Reasons it is serious (any five):
• Successful attacks on the FAA air traffic system, including one in 2006 that partially shut down air traffic data systems in Alaska.
• Intruders penetrated the Pentagon's $300 billion Joint Strike Fighter project and stole several terabytes of design and electronics data.
• Cyberspies infiltrated the U.S. electrical grid in April 2009 and left behind software programs whose purpose is unclear.
• In Iraq, insurgents intercepted Predator drone feeds using software downloaded from the Internet.
• An act of cyberwar against a critical resource — the electric grid, financial system or communication systems — would be devastating.
• Attackers are cheap to equip and almost impossible to trace, so deniability is easy.

(Arguments "against" — e.g. that most incidents so far are espionage rather than destruction, or that threats are exaggerated — are acceptable if reasoned.)
explanation:
Marking guide (5 marks):
• 1 mark for each valid reason, up to five.
• Accept real-world examples or general reasons (critical infrastructure dependence, difficulty of attribution, low cost of attack). Reasoned points 'against' also earn marks.
hint: Think of real attacks on critical systems (air traffic, defence projects, power grids) and what a successful attack could do.

body:
Cyberwarfare — attacks by states and organised groups on a nation's computer systems and critical infrastructure.

Assess the management, organization and technology factors that have created this problem.
answer:
Management — for cybercriminals and hostile states, cyberwarfare lets them compete with superpowers for a fraction of the cost of conventional warfare. As more infrastructure relies on the Internet there is no shortage of targets, and users of targeted systems are still too careless about security.

Organization — the U.S. had no clear policy on how it would respond to a catastrophic cyberattack; proposed legislation to toughen standards is likely to be insufficient, and the organization of cybersecurity is messy, with no clear leader among intelligence agencies.

Technology — technological dominance is hard to keep because the technology needed to attack is cheap. Secret surveillance software can be installed on unprotected systems and spread to others, and tracing the identity of attackers through cyberspace is next to impossible, so deniability is simple.
explanation:
Marking guide (5 marks):
• Management factor explained — 1.5 marks.
• Organization factor explained — 1.5 marks.
• Technology factor explained — 1.5 marks.
• 0.5 mark for an especially clear explanation.
hint: Give one factor under each heading: management (motives and carelessness), organization (policy and coordination), technology (cost and traceability).

body:
Cyberwarfare — attacks by states and organised groups on a nation's computer systems and critical infrastructure.

What solutions have been proposed? Do you think they will be effective? Why or why not?
answer:
Proposed solutions:
• Legislation requiring all critical-infrastructure companies to meet newer, tougher cybersecurity standards. As attack technology advances, these standards will likely be insufficient.
• Creation of Cybercom (activated May 2010) to coordinate military and government cybersecurity — protecting Pentagon networks, stock exchanges, global banking clearing and air traffic control. Insiders doubt it can organise the agencies effectively without direct access to the President.
• Entrusting some cyberwarfare work to private defence contractors, because spy agencies are barred from operating on home soil; preventing attacks may also require examining some foreign e-mail or giving intelligence agencies more access to networks and ISPs.

Effectiveness: only partly — standards lag the threat, coordination is weak, and expanded surveillance raises privacy concerns. (Accept a reasoned "yes" or "no".)
explanation:
Marking guide (5 marks):
• Proposed solutions described — 3 marks.
• Candidate's view on whether they will be effective — 1 mark.
• Reason for that view — 1 mark.
hint: Think of legislation, a coordinating command, and using private contractors — then judge each.

body:
Cyberwarfare — attacks by states and organised groups on a nation's computer systems and critical infrastructure.

Are there other solutions for this problem that should be pursued? What are they?
answer:
There are no clear-cut solutions. Offensive capabilities are closely guarded and classified, but former officials say they have grown dramatically in sophistication; because tracking attackers has proven so difficult, the best defence may be a strong offence.

Other options worth pursuing: international treaties and norms on cyberwarfare, public–private information sharing, hardening and segmenting critical infrastructure, better training and awareness for users of sensitive systems, and investment in attribution (forensics).
explanation:
Marking guide (5 marks):
• Recognising that there are no clear-cut solutions — 3 marks.
• Explaining one or more additional solutions (e.g. strong offence as defence, treaties, hardening infrastructure, training) — 2 marks.
hint: Is there a clear-cut answer? Consider offence as defence, international agreements and hardening systems.

body: Define Porter's competitive forces model and explain how it works.
answer:
Definition: Porter's competitive forces model provides a general view of the firm, its competitors and the firm's environment. It is used to understand a firm's competitive advantage — a firm's strategy is shaped by five forces acting on it.

The five forces:
1. Traditional competitors — all firms share market space with rivals who keep devising more efficient ways to produce, introducing new products and services, building brands and imposing switching costs on customers.
2. New market entrants — new companies keep entering. Some industries have very low barriers to entry (a pizza shop or small retail business); others are very hard to enter (computer chips, with very high capital costs).
3. Substitute products and services — in almost every industry there are substitutes customers can turn to if your prices become too high (ethanol for petrol; wind, solar, coal and hydro for industrial electricity).
4. Customers — profitability depends on attracting and retaining customers and charging high prices. Customer power grows when they can easily switch to a competitor or force firms to compete on price.
5. Suppliers — supplier market power hurts profits when the firm cannot raise prices as fast as its suppliers. The more suppliers a firm has, the more control it has over price, quality and delivery schedules.

How it works: the firm analyses the strength of each force and uses strategies (often IT-enabled: low-cost leadership, product differentiation, focus on market niche, customer and supplier intimacy) to counter them.
explanation:
Marking guide (12 marks):
• Definition — a general view of the firm, its competitors and its environment, used to understand competitive advantage — 2 marks.
• Each of the five forces correctly named and explained (traditional competitors, new market entrants, substitute products and services, customers, suppliers) — 2 marks each, 10 marks.
• A force named without explanation earns 1 mark. Accept equivalent names (e.g. 'threat of new entrants', 'bargaining power of buyers/suppliers', 'rivalry among existing competitors').
hint: Define it in one line, then name and explain the five forces acting on a firm.

body: Explain how the value chain model can be used to identify opportunities for information systems.
answer:
The value chain model highlights the specific activities in the business where competitive strategies and information systems will have the greatest impact. It views the firm as a series of primary and support activities that add value to products or services:
• Primary activities are directly related to production and distribution — inbound logistics, operations, outbound logistics, sales and marketing, service.
• Support activities make the primary activities possible — administration and management, human resources, technology, procurement.

Managers examine each activity to find where IS can cut costs or add value (e.g. automated warehouse systems for inbound logistics, CRM for sales and service), and can link the firm's value chain to those of its suppliers, distributors and customers.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• Explaining the value chain as a way to pinpoint activities where IS have most impact — 2 marks.
• Mentioning primary and support (secondary) activities — 2 marks.
hint: The model splits a firm into primary and support activities. Where would IS add most value?

body: How does information technology flatten organizations?
answer:
• IT broadens the distribution of information, empowering lower-level employees and increasing management efficiency.
• Lower-level employees receive the information they need to make decisions without supervision, so decision-making rights are pushed lower.
• Organizations can downsize — fewer employees and fewer levels in the hierarchy.
• The management span of control is broadened, so high-level managers can control more workers over greater distances; many firms have eliminated thousands of middle managers as a result.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• Any four well-made points about distributing information, pushing decisions down, fewer layers/middle managers and wider span of control — 1 mark each.
hint: Think about who gets information, who makes decisions, and how many managers are needed.

body: How are encryption, authentication, digital signatures and digital certificates each used to ensure security?
answer:
• Encryption — scrambles a message according to a key, sends the scrambled message, and unscrambles it at the other end with a matching key, so only the intended receiver can read it.
• Authentication — confirms the identity of a person using passwords, tokens, smart cards, biometric data or digital signatures.
• Digital signatures — digital codes attached to an electronically transmitted message, used to verify the origin and content of the message.
• Digital certificates — data files used to establish the identity of people and electronic assets for online transactions. A trusted third party (certificate authority) validates identities, using public and private encryption keys.
explanation:
Marking guide (8 marks):
• 2 marks for each of the four explained (encryption, authentication, digital signatures, digital certificates).
hint: One is about scrambling, one about proving who you are, one about proving a message's origin, one about a trusted third party.

body: Define computer crime.
answer: Computer crime is "any violation of criminal law that involves a knowledge of computer technology for its perpetration, investigation or prosecution."
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Violation of criminal law — 1 mark.
• Involving knowledge of computer technology for perpetration, investigation or prosecution — 1 mark.
hint: It is a violation of criminal law with a link to computer knowledge.

body: Provide two examples of crime in which computers are targets and two examples in which computers are used as instruments of crime.
answer:
Computers as targets (any two):
• Breaching the confidentiality of protected computerized data.
• Accessing a computer system without authority.
• Knowingly accessing a protected computer to commit fraud.
• Intentionally accessing a protected computer and causing damage.
• Knowingly transmitting a program, code or command that intentionally damages a protected computer.
• Threatening to cause damage to a protected computer.

Computers as instruments (any two):
• Theft of trade secrets.
• Unauthorized copying of software or copyrighted intellectual property (articles, books, music, video).
• Schemes to defraud.
• Using e-mail for threats or harassment.
• Intentionally intercepting electronic communication; illegally accessing stored e-mail and voice mail.
• Transmitting or possessing child pornography using a computer.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• Two valid 'computer as target' examples — 1 mark each.
• Two valid 'computer as instrument' examples — 1 mark each.
hint: Target: the computer or its data is attacked. Instrument: the computer is the tool used to commit an ordinary crime.

body: Describe the roles of firewalls, intrusion detection systems and antivirus software in promoting security.
answer:
• Firewalls — a combination of hardware and software that controls the flow of incoming and outgoing network traffic, preventing unauthorized users from accessing private networks; placed between the internal network and untrusted external networks such as the Internet.
• Intrusion detection systems — full-time monitoring tools placed at the most vulnerable points ("hot spots") of corporate networks to detect and deter intruders continually; they raise an alarm on suspicious or anomalous events.
• Antivirus software — checks computer systems and drives for viruses and other malware and often eliminates the malicious software from the infected area; it must be kept updated.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• 2 marks each for firewalls, intrusion detection systems and antivirus software, correctly described.
hint: One blocks, one watches and alarms, one scans and removes.

body: With an appropriate sketch representing each, explain the three principal network topologies.
answer:
• Star topology — all devices on the network connect to a single central hub (or switch); all traffic passes through it. Sketch: a centre node with lines out to each computer.
• Bus topology — one station transmits signals that travel in both directions along a single transmission cable; all signals are broadcast to the entire network. Sketch: one straight line (with terminators at each end) with computers attached along it.
• Ring topology — connects network components in a closed loop; messages pass from computer to computer in one direction around the loop, and only one station transmits at a time. Sketch: computers placed around a circle.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• 2 marks for each topology: the explanation and the sketch.
• The answer is typed, so accept a clear description of the sketch (e.g. 'all computers on lines out from a central hub') in place of a drawing.
hint: Star, bus and ring. For each, say how the computers are connected and how messages travel.

body: State any four principal Internet services.
answer:
Any four of:
• E-mail — person-to-person messaging; document sharing.
• Chatting and instant messaging — interactive, real-time conversations.
• Newsgroups — discussion groups on electronic bulletin boards.
• Telnet — logging on to one computer system and doing work on another.
• File Transfer Protocol (FTP) — transferring files from computer to computer.
• World Wide Web — retrieving, formatting and displaying information (text, audio, graphics, video) using hypertext links.
explanation:
Marking guide (8 marks):
• 2 marks for each of four services: 1 for naming it, 1 for a brief explanation.
hint: Think of what you can do once connected: messaging, chatting, discussion boards, remote login, file transfer, the web.

body: State and explain any three major components that can be used in any simple network.
answer:
Any three of:
• Network interface card (NIC) — built into each computer to connect it to the network's transmission medium (cable or wireless).
• Network operating system (NOS) — routes and manages communications on the network and coordinates network resources.
• Hub — a very simple device that connects network components, sending a packet of data to all other connected devices.
• Switch — more intelligent than a hub; filters and forwards data to a specified destination on the network.
• Router — a communications processor that routes packets of data through different networks, ensuring data reaches the correct address.
• Transmission medium — the connection medium, e.g. telephone wire, coaxial cable or radio signals for wireless networks.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• 2 marks each for any three components: 1 for naming, 1 for explaining.
hint: Think of what each computer needs, what manages the network, and the devices that connect and direct traffic.

body: What is the difference between information technology and information systems?
answer:
Information technology (IT) consists of all the hardware and software that a firm needs to use to achieve its business objectives.

An information system (IS) is more complex: technically, a set of interrelated components that collect (or retrieve), process, store and distribute information to support decision making and control in an organization. It includes people, procedures and organization as well as technology.

So information technology is a subset (one part) of an information system.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• Correct definition of IT — 2 marks.
• Correct definition of IS — 2 marks.
• Stating that IT is part of (a subset of) IS — 2 marks.
hint: One is the hardware and software; the other is a wider set of components that serve the organization. How are they related?

body: Outline any four functions of information systems.
answer:
• Support decision making, coordination and control in the organization.
• Help managers and employees analyse problems.
• Help them visualize complex subjects.
• Help create new products.
(Also acceptable: input, processing, output and feedback of information; storing and distributing information.)
explanation:
Marking guide (8 marks):
• 2 marks each for any four valid functions, briefly explained.
hint: What do IS help managers and employees do beyond just storing data?

body: Define operational excellence and explain how information systems can help achieve it.
answer:
Operational excellence is the achievement of higher levels of productivity, efficiency and profitability in business operations.

IS help by improving communication with suppliers and optimizing the supply chain, helping managers communicate with workers more efficiently, enabling technological innovation in products, minimizing warehouse overhead and streamlining distribution (e.g. Walmart's RetailLink).
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• Definition — 2 marks.
• How IS help achieve it — 2 marks (any two valid ways).
hint: Define it in terms of productivity and efficiency, then give ways IS improve efficiency.

body: You work for an auto manufacturer and distributor. How could you use information systems to achieve greater customer intimacy?
answer: Create a website where customers can customize cars and communicate with support staff and other owners; send automated e-mail reminders for periodic check-ups; and track customer preferences by area so you supply cars that reflect local needs and desires.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Any two sensible IS-based ideas for knowing and serving customers better — 1 mark each.
hint: Think of ways to know your car owners better and keep in touch with them.

body:
CASE STUDY: BYOD — A SECURITY NIGHTMARE?

Bring your own device has become a huge trend, with half of employees with mobile computing tools at workplaces worldwide using their own devices. This figure is expected to increase even more in the years to come. But while use of the iPhone, iPad, and other mobile computing devices in the workplace is growing, so are security problems. Quite a few security experts believe that smartphones and other mobile devices now pose one of the most serious security threats for organizations today.

Whether mobile devices are company-assigned or employee-owned, they are opening up new avenues for accessing corporate data that need to be closely monitored and protected. Sensitive data on mobile devices travel, both physically and electronically, from the office to home and possibly other off-site locations. According to a February 2016 Ponemon Institute study of 588 U.S. IT and security professionals, 67 percent of those surveyed reported that it was certain or likely that an employee’s mobile access to confidential corporate data had resulted in a data breach. Unfortunately, only 41 percent of respondents said their companies had policies for accessing corporate data from mobile devices.

More than half of security breaches occur when devices are lost or stolen. That puts all of the personal and corporate data stored on the device, as well as access to corporate data on remote servers, at risk. Physical access to mobile devices may be a greater threat than hacking into a network because less effort is required to gain entry. Experienced attackers can easily circumvent passwords or locks on mobile devices or access encrypted data. Moreover, many smartphone users leave their phones totally unprotected to begin with or fail to keep the security features of their devices up-to-date. In the Websense and the Ponemon Institute’s Global Study on Mobility Risks, 59 percent of respondents reported that employees circumvented or disabled security features such as passwords and key locks.

Another worry today is large-scale data leakage caused by use of cloud computing services. Employees are increasingly using public cloud services such as Google Drive or Dropbox for file sharing and collaboration. There are many instances where employees are using Dropbox to store and exchange files without their employers’ approval. In early 2015 Dropbox had to patch a security flaw that allowed cyberattackers to steal new information uploaded to accounts through compromised third-party apps that work with Dropbox services on Android devices. There is very little a company can do to prevent employees who are allowed to use their smartphones from downloading corporate data so they can work on those data remotely.

Text messaging and other mobile messaging technologies are being used to deliver all kinds of scam campaigns, such as adult content and rogue pharmacy, phishing, and banking scams, and text messages have been a propagation medium for Trojan horses and worms. A malicious source is now able to send a text message that will open in a mobile browser by default, which can be readily utilized to exploit the recipient.

To date, deliberate hacker attacks on mobile devices have been limited in scope and impact, but this situation is worsening. Android is now the world’s most popular operating system for mobile devices with 81 percent of the global market, and most mobile malware is targeted at the Android platform. When corporate and personal data are stored on the same device, mobile malware unknowingly installed by the user could find its way onto the corporate network.

Apple uses a closed “walled garden” model for managing its apps and reviews each one before releasing it on its App Store. CASE STUDY: MWEB BUSINESS — HACKED

MWEB, launched in 1997, became South Africa’s leading ISP in 1998. It has established itself as a company that provides a cutting-edge network and service infrastructure and outstanding customer service. Currently, MWEB’s customer base of 320,000 includes home users; small, medium, and large business customers; and corporate clients. MWEB won the ISP of the Year award at the MyBroadband Conference in Johannesburg in 2010. The award was based on the performance of its various broadband services as well as on customer satisfaction.

Its business division, MWEB Business, was founded in January 1998. MWEB Business prides itself as being a business partner that is perfectly positioned to leverage the power of Web-based technologies in all areas of an organization. MWEB Business helps companies:
• Manage business data in ways that add real value and insight to their operations.
• Integrate existing systems with the Internet so as to close the gap between technology, strategy, and the organization’s bottom line.
• Develop, manage, and maintain solutions that include all aspects of Internet connectivity, Web site development and hosting, broadband and wireless applications, e-commerce, and consultancy services.
• Manage internal information among employees, as well as among business partners and suppliers.

MWEB has moved forward in publicizing its plans for the South African Internet market. According to MWEB CEO, the company needs to improve the quality of their network, which is not only an MWEB problem, but also a general telecommunication network problem. Despite having a less-than-ideal network infrastructure, MWEB uses AVG Internet Security to offer its customers the best possible security while online. AVG Internet Security offers MWEB customers the following features:
• Identity protection for safe banking and shopping
• Link Scanner for safe surfing and searching
• Web Shield for safe social networking, chatting, and downloading
• Antiphishing and antispam for a safe uncluttered inbox
• High-speed antivirus/antispyware software with automatic updates
• An enhanced firewall

In addition, MWEB automatically protects customers against junk email and viruses that are sent via email. Its virus filter ensures that only virus-free email is delivered to clients’ inboxes by automatically cleaning e-mails from recognized malware sources. MWEB advises its customers to keep their ADSL connections (Internet connections) safe from bandwidth theft and account abuse by blocking unsolicited incoming connections to network ports commonly used by hackers.

Despite the multitude of security services offered by MWEB, a number of MWEB Business subscribers’ account details were compromised when their logon and password details were published on the Internet by hackers. Initial reports indicated that as many as 2,390 users of MWEB’s business digital subscriber lines were affected. The company disclosed the security breach on October 25, 2010. It appears that hackers gained access to the Internet Solutions’ self-service management system that MWEB Business uses to provide and manage business accounts that have not yet been migrated to the MWEB network.

Historically, MWEB Business was a reseller of Internet Solutions’ Uncapped & Fixed IP ADSL services, which were provisioned and managed by MWEB using a Web-based management interface provided by Internet Solutions. All new Business ADSL services provided after April 2010, as well as the bulk of legacy services already migrated, used MWEB’s internal authentication systems, which were completely unaffected by this incident.

MWEB responded quickly to the hacking incident. According to the CEO, about 1,000 clients on the Internet Solutions network needed to be migrated from the old server which was attacked by hackers. Although the network was quickly secured, most customers had recently been moved to MWEB’s IPC network. MWEB would also be contacting these customers to reset their passwords, as an added security measure. The CEO was quick to note that no personal information was lost and that none of MWEB’s clients suffered any losses as their usernames and passwords had been recreated and changed. He further added that MWEB successfully repels 5,000 attacks a day.

The general manager of MWEB Business, emphasized that only ADSL authentication usernames and passwords had been compromised. The integrity of the personal or private data related to the accounts remained intact, as did the access credentials for each customer’s bundled onsite router. The general manager did acknowledge the seriousness of the hack, apologizing for any inconvenience the breach may have caused to MWEB’s customers. As soon as the breach was identified, MWEB took immediate action to evaluate the extent of the breach and to limit any damage. In MWEB’s defense, the CEO said that MWEB constantly advises its customers to be vigilant regarding their online data and security. In addition, MWEB was working closely with Internet Solutions to investigate the nature and source of the breach to ensure that it does not happen again.

———

What technology issues led to the security breach at MWEB?
answer:
• MWEB Business subscribers' account (logon and password) details were compromised and published on the Internet by hackers — the authentication data was not adequately protected. (5 marks)
• Hackers got in through the older, outsourced web-based self-service management system of Internet Solutions, which MWEB still used for business accounts not yet migrated to MWEB's own, more secure network and authentication systems. (5 marks)
explanation:
Marking guide (10 marks):
• Compromised logon and password details published by hackers — 5 marks.
• The legacy Internet Solutions self-service system that had not yet been migrated to the more secure MWEB network — 5 marks.
hint: Where exactly did the hackers get in, and why was that system still in use?

According to MWEB CEO, the company needs to improve the quality of their network, which is not only an MWEB problem, but also a general telecommunication network problem. Despite having a less-than-ideal network infrastructure, MWEB uses AVG Internet Security to offer its customers the best possible security while online. AVG Internet Security offers MWEB customers the following features:
• Identity protection for safe banking and shopping
• Link Scanner for safe surfing and searching
• Web Shield for safe social networking, chatting, and downloading
• Antiphishing and antispam for a safe uncluttered inbox
• High-speed antivirus/antispyware software with automatic updates
• An enhanced firewall

In addition, MWEB automatically protects customers against junk email and viruses that are sent via email. Its virus filter ensures that only virus-free email is delivered to clients’ inboxes by automatically cleaning e-mails from recognized malware sources. MWEB advises its customers to keep their ADSL connections (Internet connections) safe from bandwidth theft and account abuse by blocking unsolicited incoming connections to network ports commonly used by hackers.

Despite the multitude of security services offered by MWEB, a number of MWEB Business subscribers’ account details were compromised when their logon and password details were published on the Internet by hackers. Initial reports indicated that as many as 2,390 users of MWEB’s business digital subscriber lines were affected. The company disclosed the security breach on October 25, 2010. It appears that hackers gained access to the Internet Solutions’ self-service management system that MWEB Business uses to provide and manage business accounts that have not yet been migrated to the MWEB network.

Historically, MWEB Business was a reseller of Internet Solutions’ Uncapped & Fixed IP ADSL services, which were provisioned and managed by MWEB using a Web-based management interface provided by Internet Solutions. All new Business ADSL services provided after April 2010, as well as the bulk of legacy services already migrated, used MWEB’s internal authentication systems, which were completely unaffected by this incident.

MWEB responded quickly to the hacking incident. According to the CEO, about 1,000 clients on the Internet Solutions network needed to be migrated from the old server which was attacked by hackers. Although the network was quickly secured, most customers had recently been moved to MWEB’s IPC network. MWEB would also be contacting these customers to reset their passwords, as an added security measure. The CEO was quick to note that no personal information was lost and that none of MWEB’s clients suffered any losses as their usernames and passwords had been recreated and changed. He further added that MWEB successfully repels 5,000 attacks a day.

The general manager of MWEB Business, emphasized that only ADSL authentication usernames and passwords had been compromised. The integrity of the personal or private data related to the accounts remained intact, as did the access credentials for each customer’s bundled onsite router. The general manager did acknowledge the seriousness of the hack, apologizing for any inconvenience the breach may have caused to MWEB’s customers. As soon as the breach was identified, MWEB took immediate action to evaluate the extent of the breach and to limit any damage. In MWEB’s defense, the CEO said that MWEB constantly advises its customers to be vigilant regarding their online data and security. In addition, MWEB was working closely with Internet Solutions to investigate the nature and source of the breach to ensure that it does not happen again.

———

What should MWEB do in the future to avoid similar incidents?
answer:
Any four of:
• Improve identity management (stronger authentication, multi-factor login).
• Implement up-to-date security devices and protocols — digital certificates, intrusion detection systems, MIS audits.
• Undertake regular and thorough security testing.
• Proactively evaluate the extent of any breach immediately and limit damage.
• Keep advising customers to be vigilant about their online data and security.
• Work closely with partners such as Internet Solutions to investigate breaches — and complete migration off legacy systems.
explanation:
Marking guide (10 marks):
• 2.5 marks each for any four valid, explained measures.
hint: Think of identity management, up-to-date security technology, testing and audits, and customer awareness.

body: Explain the six strategic business objectives of investing in information systems.
answer:
1. Operational excellence — firms continuously seek to improve the efficiency of their operations to achieve higher profitability. IS and technologies are among the most important tools for higher efficiency and productivity, especially when coupled with changes in business practices and management behaviour.
2. New products, services and business models — IS are a major enabling tool for firms to create new products and services and entirely new business models.
3. Customer and supplier intimacy — when a business really knows and serves its customers well, they return and buy more, raising revenues and profits. Likewise, the more a business engages its suppliers, the better they can provide vital inputs.
4. Improved decision making — IS give managers the right information at the right time (including real-time data from the marketplace) to make informed decisions.
5. Competitive advantage — when firms achieve one or more of the above, they have usually achieved a competitive advantage: doing things better than competitors, charging less for superior products and responding to customers and suppliers in real time.
6. Survival — firms also invest in IS because they are necessities of doing business, sometimes driven by industry-level changes (e.g. ATMs in banking) or by government regulation and reporting requirements.
explanation:
Marking guide (12 marks):
• 2 marks each for the six objectives, named and explained: operational excellence; new products, services and business models; customer and supplier intimacy; improved decision making; competitive advantage; survival.
hint: Efficiency, innovation, closeness to customers and suppliers, decisions, beating rivals, and staying alive.

body: What are complementary assets?
answer: Complementary assets are the assets required to derive value from a primary investment. For example, to realize value from automobiles you need substantial complementary investments in highways, roads and petrol stations. For IS, they are the organizational and management investments (processes, culture, training) that make the technology pay off.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Definition: assets required to derive value from a primary investment — 1 mark.
• A valid example or application to IS — 1 mark.
hint: Assets you need alongside a primary investment to get value from it.

body: Why are complementary assets essential for ensuring that information systems provide genuine value for an organization?
answer:
To obtain meaningful value from information systems, organizations must support their technology investments with appropriate complementary investments in organization and management.

Research shows that firms that support technology investments with complementary assets — new business models, new business processes, management behaviour, organizational culture, training — receive superior returns, while firms that fail to make these investments receive little or no return on their IT investments. Examples of complementary assets: organizational (supportive culture, efficient processes, decentralized authority), managerial (strong senior support, incentives for innovation, training), and social (Internet infrastructure, standards, laws).
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• Marks awarded on closeness to the scheme: technology must be supported by organizational and management investments (2), research evidence that such firms earn superior returns while others earn little (2), examples of complementary assets (2).
hint: Technology alone rarely pays off. What else must a firm invest in, and what does research show?

body: Modern businesses are gradually shifting towards digital platforms for buying and selling. Discuss any five unique features that are propelling the use of e-commerce in the global economy.
answer:
Any five of:
• Ubiquity — Internet/web technology is available everywhere (work, home, mobile), any time. The marketplace is extended beyond traditional boundaries into a "marketspace"; shopping costs fall and convenience rises.
• Global reach — the technology reaches across national boundaries; commerce is enabled across cultures and borders seamlessly. The marketspace potentially includes billions of consumers and millions of businesses.
• Universal standards — one set of technology standards (Internet standards) shared by all nations, so disparate computer systems communicate easily; market entry and search costs fall.
• Richness — video, audio and text messages can be integrated into a single marketing message and consumer experience.
• Interactivity — the technology allows two-way communication between merchant and consumer; the consumer becomes a participant in delivering goods to the market.
• Information density — information collection, storage, processing and communication costs drop dramatically while currency, accuracy and timeliness improve; prices and costs become more transparent.
• Personalization/customization — messages can be targeted to individuals (by name, interests, clickstream and past purchases) and products customized to user preferences.
• Social technology — the technology supports user content generation and social networking.
explanation:
Marking guide (15 marks):
• 3 marks each for any five features: name the feature and explain its business significance.
hint: Think of 'anywhere, anytime', worldwide, shared standards, rich media, two-way, cheap information, tailored messages, social.

body: What is the positive impact of disintermediation in e-commerce transactions?
answer:
Disintermediation is the removal of intermediaries from a supply chain — "cutting out the middlemen" in a transaction — or the removal of organizations or business process layers responsible for intermediary steps in a value chain.

Positive impact: by selling directly to consumers or reducing the number of intermediaries, companies raise profits while charging lower prices. Goods sold online are usually cheaper than in traditional markets because firms no longer pay commissions to agents, distributors or retailers, which lowers operating costs and translates into cheaper goods and services for customers.
explanation:
Marking guide (5 marks):
• Explanation of disintermediation — 2 marks.
• Its impact in e-commerce (lower costs, lower prices, higher profits) — 3 marks.
hint: Define it ('cutting out the middlemen'), then say what that does to costs and prices.

body:
Explain how the following mediating factors influence information systems and organizations:
• business processes
• politics
• culture
• surrounding environment
answer:
• Business processes — business processes are the actual way firms produce value; they are collections of routines (standard operating procedures): precise rules, procedures and practices developed to cope with expected situations. Processes shape the kind of IS an organization adopts, and new IS change those routines.
• Politics — people occupy different positions with different specialties, concerns and perspectives, so they have divergent views on how resources, rewards and punishments should be distributed. This produces political struggle, competition and conflict, and resistance to IS that change who has power or information.
• Culture — the bedrock, unquestioned assumptions that define an organization's goals and products: what it should produce, how, where and for whom. Business processes are embedded in the culture; IS that fit the culture are adopted easily, those that challenge it meet resistance.
• Surrounding environment — organizations draw resources from, and supply goods and services to, their environment. The relationship is reciprocal: organizations depend on the social and physical environment around them, and they also try to influence it (alliances to influence politics, advertising to shape customer acceptance). Environmental change (competition, regulation, technology) drives what IS a firm needs.
explanation:
Marking guide (8 marks):
• 2 marks for each of the four factors, well explained and linked to IS adoption.
hint: For each, say what it is in an organization and how it shapes (or is shaped by) the IS adopted.

body: Discuss any five principal e-commerce business models and their corresponding revenue models.
answer:
Any five:
• E-tailer — sells physical products directly to consumers or individual businesses (e.g. Amazon, Jumia). Revenue: sales, advertising, affiliate.
• Transaction broker — saves users money and time by processing online sales transactions, charging a fee each time (e.g. online travel or brokerage). Revenue: transaction fees, advertising.
• Market creator — provides a digital environment where buyers and sellers meet, search, display products and set prices; serves consumers or B2B (e.g. eBay). Revenue: transaction fees, advertising.
• Content provider — provides digital content such as news, music, photos or video over the web. Revenue: sales, advertising, subscription.
• Community provider — an online meeting place where people with similar interests communicate and find information (e.g. Facebook). Revenue: advertising, affiliate.
• Portal — an initial point of entry to the web with specialized content and services (e.g. Yahoo). Revenue: advertising, affiliate, subscription.
• Service provider — provides applications such as photo or video sharing and user-generated content as services, plus services like online storage and backup (e.g. Google Drive). Revenue: subscription, free/freemium, affiliate.

Revenue models in brief: advertising (audience exposed to ads); sales (selling goods, information or services); subscription (ongoing fee for access); free/freemium (basic free, premium paid); transaction fee (fee for enabling a transaction); affiliate (referral fee or share of sales).
explanation:
Marking guide (20 marks):
• For each of five models: 3 marks for a well-explained business model and 1 mark for correctly identifying its revenue model(s).
• Explaining the revenue models themselves is not required.
hint: E-tailer, transaction broker, market creator, content provider, community provider, portal, service provider — and how each earns money.

body: Suppose your business had an e-commerce website where it sold goods and accepted credit card and mobile money payments. Discuss the major security threats to this website and their potential impact.
answer:
Digital data are vulnerable to destruction, misuse, error, fraud and hardware or software failure. Any four threats, each with its impact:
• Internet vulnerability — the Internet is an open system, making the site and internal systems vulnerable to outsiders; data can be stolen or altered.
• Hackers and denial-of-service (DoS) attacks — can flood or penetrate the site, causing outages, lost sales and stolen customer data.
• Fraud from internal and external sources — credit card and mobile money fraud, stolen card details, insider fraud; financial loss, chargebacks and reputational damage.
• Wireless security challenges — Wi-Fi networks penetrated with sniffer programs to gain access to network resources.
• Malware — viruses, worms and Trojans can disable systems and the website or steal payment data.
• Software vulnerabilities — bugs that cannot all be eliminated and can be exploited by hackers.
• Cloud computing — dispersed resources make it hard to track unauthorized activity or apply controls.
• End-user errors — mistakes that corrupt data or expose systems.
explanation:
Marking guide (12 marks):
• Candidates should identify at least four sources of threat.
• 3 marks for each well-explained threat with its potential impact.
hint: At least four threats: the open Internet, hackers and DoS, fraud, wireless, malware, software bugs, cloud, user error. Say what each could do to the business.

body: Explain any four ways of minimizing the security threats to an e-commerce website that accepts credit card and mobile money payments.
answer:
Any four of:
• Firewalls — prevent unauthorized users from accessing the private network when linked to the Internet.
• Intrusion detection systems — monitor networks for suspicious traffic and attempts to access systems.
• Identity management — passwords, tokens, smart cards and biometric authentication to verify users.
• Antivirus and antispyware software — detect and remove viruses, worms and spyware.
• Encryption — scramble data (e.g. SSL/TLS) to secure transmissions and stored payment data.
• Digital certificates with public key encryption — authenticate identities in electronic transactions.
• Fault-tolerant computer systems — keep the site available.
• Software metrics and rigorous testing — improve software quality and reliability.
explanation:
Marking guide (8 marks):
• 2 marks each for any four well-explained measures.
hint: Think of tools that block, monitor, authenticate, scan, encrypt and keep systems available.

body:
Case study: Monitoring employees on networks — unethical or good business?

State and explain any four reasons why managers should monitor employee e-mail and Internet usage.
answer:
Any four of:
• Lost time and productivity — employees focusing on personal rather than company business.
• Lost revenue — too much time on personal business translates into lost revenue.
• Network congestion — heavy personal traffic (streaming, downloading multimedia) can clog the company network so legitimate work cannot be done.
• Leakage of confidential information and trade secrets through e-mail or social networks, embarrassing the company and benefiting competitors.
• Legal liability and reputation — when employees use e-mail or the web at work or on company equipment, anything they do, including anything illegal, carries the company's name.
explanation:
Marking guide (12 marks):
• 3 marks each for any four well-explained reasons.
hint: Think of productivity, revenue, network capacity, leaks of confidential information, and legal liability.

body:
Case study: Monitoring employees on networks — unethical or good business?

Should managers inform employees that their web behaviour is being monitored, or should employees be monitored secretly? Explain your answer.
answer:
Managers should inform employees that their web usage is monitored, because:
• Every organization is expected to have an Internet usage policy stating what is expected of employees — monitoring should be part of it.
• When employees know their computers are monitored, they avoid personal business (Facebook, online games) during work hours — monitoring then works as a deterrent.
• Employees concentrate more on their work, helping the company achieve its goals, and trust is preserved because nothing is hidden.

(This is an open question; a well-argued case for secret monitoring can also earn marks.)
explanation:
Marking guide (10 marks):
• Open question — assessors use discretion where answers differ from the scheme.
• 5 marks each for any two well-explained points supporting the candidate's position.
hint: Take a side and give two reasons. Think about policies, deterrence and trust.

body:
Case study: Monitoring employees on networks — unethical or good business?

Is it ethical for a company to fire an employee based on the content of their personal social media platform? Explain your answer.
answer:
This is open; marks go to the arguments raised. Guiding points:
• Yes, where there is a social media policy — because posts can harm a business, many firms set rules (no social media at work, limits on content, not linking the company to political stances or causes). An employee who breaks the policy can face action including dismissal, and the firm is justified.
• Yes, even without a policy — employees are still expected not to tarnish the organization's image; if their actions dent its image, dismissal can be ethical.
• No — another school of thought treats social media posts as free speech; no one should be held liable for their posts, especially when made after working hours, so using them against an employee would be unethical.
explanation:
Marking guide (10 marks):
• Open question: marks awarded on the arguments raised.
• Expect a clear position supported by points such as the existence of a social media policy, harm to the company's image, and free speech / after-hours posting.
hint: Consider social media policies, the company's image, and the free-speech/after-hours argument.

body:
Case study: Monitoring employees on networks — unethical or good business?

Describe an effective e-mail and web use policy for a company.
answer:
• It must be carefully designed and clearly communicated to everyone who uses the company's e-mail and Internet resources.
• It should detail exactly what types of activity are acceptable and what is not allowed (e.g. personal e-mail, social media, games, downloads, offensive content, sending confidential data outside), including whether and when personal use is allowed.
• It should state that use is monitored and how.
• It should clearly set out the sanctions that will follow for each offence against the policy.
explanation:
Marking guide (8 marks):
• Designed and communicated to all users — up to 4 marks.
• Details acceptable and unacceptable activity, monitoring and clear sanctions for offences — up to 4 marks.
hint: What should it say, and how should it be communicated and enforced?

body:
Quainoo & Co Company Limited has automated its business processes, moved its operations to the Internet, and receives online payments for goods and services.

Mr. Jay, the CEO, has asked you, a senior officer, to explain five reasons why this new way of doing business online is vulnerable to error, destruction and abuse.
answer:
When large amounts of data are stored electronically and interconnected through networks, they face many more threats than in manual form. Any five:
• Internet vulnerabilities — large public networks are open to anyone; once the Internet is part of the corporate network, systems are exposed to outsiders.
• Wireless security challenges — radio frequency bands are easy to scan; Bluetooth and Wi-Fi are susceptible to eavesdroppers.
• Malicious software — viruses, worms and Trojan horses (a virus attaches itself to other programs or files and executes without the user's knowledge).
• Hackers and computer crime — hackers and crackers exploit weaknesses in website and system security.
• Internal threats from employees — insiders have privileged access and, with sloppy internal procedures, can roam systems without leaving a trace.
• Software vulnerability — software errors and flaws, growing with program size and complexity, cause losses and can be exploited.
explanation:
Marking guide (10 marks):
• 2 marks each for any five well-explained reasons.
hint: Think of open networks, wireless, malware, hackers, insiders and software bugs.

body:
Quainoo & Co Company Limited has automated its business processes, moved its operations to the Internet, and receives online payments.

State and explain any five tools and technologies the company can use to safeguard its information systems.
answer:
Any five:
• Identity management and authentication — software that tracks users and their privileges, giving each a unique digital identity; authentication by password, token, smart card or biometrics.
• Firewalls — hardware and software controlling incoming and outgoing network traffic, placed between the private network and untrusted networks like the Internet.
• Intrusion detection systems — full-time monitoring at network "hot spots" that raise an alarm on suspicious events.
• Antivirus and antispyware software — prevent, detect and remove malware.
• Unified threat management (UTM) systems — combine firewall, VPN, intrusion detection, web content filtering and antispam in one appliance to cut cost and improve manageability.
• Encryption — transforms plain text into cipher text that only the sender and intended receiver can read, protecting stored and transmitted data.
explanation:
Marking guide (10 marks):
• 2 marks each for any five well-explained tools or technologies.
hint: Authentication, firewalls, intrusion detection, antivirus, unified threat management, encryption.

Marking guide (20 marks):

body: Explain the four generic IT-enabled strategies that any firm can implement to deal with Porter's competitive forces in its industry.
answer:
• Low-cost leadership — use IS to achieve the lowest operational costs and the lowest prices (e.g. Walmart's continuous replenishment).
• Product differentiation — use IS to enable new products and services, or greatly change customer convenience in using existing ones.
• Focus on market niche — use IS to enable a specific market focus and serve this narrow target market better than competitors (customer data analysis).

Marking guide (8 marks):
