body: As the manager of a new firm, explain any four mediating factors that can influence the interaction between information systems and your organization.
answer:
Any four of:
• Organizational environment — organizations draw resources from, and supply goods and services to, their environment. The relationship is reciprocal: organizations depend on the social and physical environment around them, and they also try to influence it (alliances to influence politics, advertising to shape customer acceptance). Environmental change (competition, regulation, technology) drives what IS a firm needs.
• Organizational structure — every organization has a structure or shape (entrepreneurial, machine bureaucracy, divisionalized, professional, adhocracy). The kind of information systems a firm has, and the problems it has with them, often reflect its structure.
• Business processes and routines — business processes are the actual way firms produce value; they are collections of routines (standard operating procedures): precise rules, procedures and practices developed to cope with expected situations. Processes shape the kind of IS an organization adopts, and new IS change those routines.
• Organizational politics — people occupy different positions with different specialties, concerns and perspectives, so they have divergent views on how resources, rewards and punishments should be distributed. This produces political struggle, competition and conflict, and resistance to IS that change who has power or information.
• Organizational culture — the bedrock, unquestioned assumptions that define an organization's goals and products: what it should produce, how, where and for whom. Business processes are embedded in the culture; IS that fit the culture are adopted easily, those that challenge it meet resistance.
explanation:
Marking guide (12 marks):
• 3 marks each for any four well-explained factors.
hint: Environment, structure, business processes, politics, culture.

body: With an appropriate example each, explain the three major categories of e-commerce.
answer:
• Business-to-consumer (B2C) — retailing products and services to individual shoppers. Example: Amazon, AliExpress, Jumia.
• Business-to-business (B2B) — sales of goods and services among businesses. Example: Alibaba.
• Consumer-to-consumer (C2C) — consumers selling directly to consumers. Example: eBay, Tonaton, OLX.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• For each category: 1 mark for the definition, 1 mark for an appropriate example.
hint: Who sells to whom? Businesses, consumers, or both.

body: E-commerce technologies are much richer and more powerful than earlier technology revolutions such as radio, television and the telephone. Explain any five unique features of e-commerce that make it outstanding.
answer:
Any five of:
• Ubiquity — Internet/web technology is available everywhere (work, home, mobile), any time. The marketplace is extended beyond traditional boundaries into a "marketspace"; shopping costs fall and convenience rises.
• Global reach — the technology reaches across national boundaries; commerce is enabled across cultures and borders seamlessly. The marketspace potentially includes billions of consumers and millions of businesses.
• Universal standards — one set of technology standards (Internet standards) shared by all nations, so disparate computer systems communicate easily; market entry and search costs fall.
• Richness — video, audio and text messages can be integrated into a single marketing message and consumer experience.
• Interactivity — the technology allows two-way communication between merchant and consumer; the consumer becomes a participant in delivering goods to the market.
• Information density — information collection, storage, processing and communication costs drop dramatically while currency, accuracy and timeliness improve; prices and costs become more transparent.
• Personalization/customization — messages can be targeted to individuals (by name, interests, clickstream and past purchases) and products customized to user preferences.
• Social technology — the technology supports user content generation and social networking.
explanation:
Marking guide (10 marks):
• 2 marks each for any five well-explained features.
hint: Anywhere-anytime, worldwide, shared standards, rich media, two-way, cheap information, tailored messages.

body:
Explain any two of the following e-commerce revenue models:
• subscription
• free/freemium
• transaction fee
answer:
• Subscription — a website offering content or services charges a subscription fee for access to some or all of its offerings on an ongoing basis; often used by content providers (e.g. Netflix).
• Free/freemium — basic services or content are free, with a premium charged for advanced or special features (e.g. Google's free apps with paid premium services).
• Transaction fee — a company receives a fee for enabling or executing a transaction (e.g. eBay charges a seller a small fee when an item sells).
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• 2 marks each for any two models correctly explained.
hint: For each, say who pays, for what, and give an example.

body:
Your company is moving into a computer-based environment to stay competitive. At a management meeting you are asked to explain the following components of a simple computer network:
• Network operating system (NOS)
• Router
• Switch
• Server
answer:
• Network operating system (NOS) — routes and manages communications on the network and coordinates network resources; it can run on every computer or mainly on a dedicated server.
• Router — a communications processor that forwards packets of data between networks, ensuring data reaches the correct address; routers direct traffic on the Internet.
• Switch — a device that provides a central connection point for cables in a network and forwards data to the specific destination device.
• Server — the computer that controls or manages the network and provides shared services and resources to client computers.
explanation:
Marking guide (8 marks):
• 2 marks each for the four components, well explained.
hint: Software that manages the network; a device that forwards packets between networks; a central connection point; the computer that manages resources.

body:
Differentiate among the following terms used to describe corporate networks:
• Internet
• Intranet
• Extranet
answer:
• Internet — a global network of interconnected networks, open to the public.
• Intranet — an internal, private network a company uses to connect its own computers and share information with employees, built on Internet technology.
• Extranet — an internal network that authorised outsiders (suppliers, customers, partners) can access externally; an extension of the company's intranet.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• 2 marks each for a correct description of Internet, intranet and extranet.
hint: Global and public; private and internal; private but opened to selected outsiders.

body: A client computer connected to the Internet has access to a variety of services. State and explain any three main services/capabilities of the Internet.
answer:
Any three of:
• E-mail — person-to-person messaging; document sharing.
• Chatting and instant messaging — interactive, real-time conversations.
• Newsgroups — discussion groups on electronic bulletin boards.
• Telnet — logging on to one computer system and doing work on another.
• File Transfer Protocol (FTP) — transferring files from computer to computer.
• World Wide Web — retrieving, formatting and displaying information (text, audio, graphics, video) using hypertext links.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• 2 marks each for any three services, named and explained.
hint: Messaging, chat, discussion groups, remote login, file transfer, the web.

body: Differentiate between credit card fraud and identity theft.
answer:
Credit card fraud is a possible consequence of identity theft: a thief steals your credit card information and uses it to make purchases in a store or online.

Identity theft goes much further: it is stealing a person's personal information to open new lines of credit or new credit cards, or obtain false IDs, in that person's name.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Credit card fraud: using stolen card details for purchases — 1 mark.
• Identity theft: stealing personal information to act in the victim's name (new credit, cards, IDs) — 1 mark.
hint: One is about misusing a card; the other is about using your whole identity.

body: Which of these offenders — credit card fraudster or identity thief — is likely to be caught more easily? Give one reason for your answer.
answer: The credit card fraudster is likely to be caught more easily. Card fraud transactions can look suspicious and are flagged by the card issuer, and the thief has only limited information. Identity theft uses far more sophisticated tactics that go well beyond paying for items with a stolen card number, which makes identity thieves hard to catch early.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Choosing the credit card fraudster — 1 mark.
• A valid reason (suspicious transactions are detected; limited information vs sophisticated identity theft tactics) — 2 marks.
hint: Which one leaves suspicious transactions that banks can spot quickly?

body: Which of these offenders — credit card fraudster or identity thief — is likely to cause more harm to the victim? Give one reason for your answer.
answer: Identity theft causes more harm. It can take many forms — thieves stealing medical information to get free healthcare, or using personal information to open new lines of credit — and there is no limit to liability, so the victim may end up paying for all the damage the identity thief causes.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Choosing identity theft — 1 mark.
• A valid reason (many forms of misuse, no limit to liability, long-lasting impact) — 2 marks.
hint: Which crime can spread beyond one card, and who pays for the damage?

body: Which of these — credit card fraud or identity theft — is more difficult to protect against?
answer: Identity theft is more difficult to protect against. The credit industry has many fraud-prevention measures that limit damage from card fraud, whereas identity theft tactics are sophisticated and their impact can last for years or decades — with medical identity theft, for example, you may not realise you are a victim until a collections agency calls.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Choosing identity theft with a valid reason — 2 marks (1 mark for the choice without a reason).
hint: The credit industry has built-in protections for one of them.

body: What is cyberstalking?
answer: Cyberstalking is using the Internet and other technologies to harass or stalk another person online — e.g. posting derogatory comments, or posting the victim's phone number and e-mail on sites so that others send messages or calls to the victim.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Using the Internet/technology — 1 mark.
• To harass or stalk another person — 1 mark.
hint: Stalking, but through the Internet and other technologies.

body: With cyberstalking, give one reason why you think the offender has the advantage over the victim.
answer: The offender can sit anywhere in the world, often anonymously, and harass the victim, while the victim has no control over what the offender does or posts.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• A valid reason, explained (location independence/anonymity; victim has no control) — 2 marks.
hint: Where can the offender be, and what control does the victim have?

body: Stalking by e-mail and stalking through the Internet: which of these is the more serious form of cyberstalking? Give one reason for your answer.
answer: Internet stalking is more serious. It can be used to slander and endanger victims before a much wider audience — it takes on a 'public' dimension — while e-mail stalking reaches a limited audience and stays 'private'.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Internet stalking — 1 mark.
• Reason: wider/public audience vs e-mail's limited/private reach — 1 mark.
hint: Which one reaches a wider audience?

body: Social networking sites such as Facebook, X (Twitter), Instagram and many others are becoming media for cyberstalking. As an expert, suggest two ways this problem can be addressed.
answer:
Suggestions could include (any two):
Policies and laws:
• Punishment for sending offensive messages through communication services.
• Punishment for breach of confidentiality and privacy.
• Punishment for disclosure of information in breach of lawful contract.
What users should do:
• Strengthen devices with strong passwords or, better, multi-factor authentication.
• Keep all software updated to prevent information leaks.
• Mask their IP address with a virtual private network (VPN).
• Strengthen privacy settings on social media.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• 2 marks each for any two valid suggestions, explained.
• This part appears in the marking scheme as Q Biv; it was not printed on the question paper.
hint: Think of laws and punishments, and of what users can do to protect themselves.

body: What is the difference between an 'angel hacker', a 'gray hacker' and a 'dark hacker'?
answer: Angel (white hat) hackers probe cybersecurity weaknesses to help organizations build stronger security. Dark (black hat) hackers are motivated by malicious intent. Gray hat hackers operate in between: they are not malicious, but not always ethical either (e.g. breaking in without permission and then reporting the flaw).
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• 1 mark each for correctly describing the angel, gray and dark hacker.
hint: White hat, gray hat and black hat — what motivates each?

body: State two reasons why the Internet is vulnerable and subject to abuse.
answer:
Any two:
• The Internet is very complex and accessible to a huge number of users, which increases the likelihood of misconfigurations, flaws and unwanted network access.
• Increased connectivity — so many remote devices connected to networks creates new access points for attacks.
• It is an open system by design, with fixed addresses and always-on connections that make targets easy to find; other valid reasons are accepted.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Any two valid reasons, explained — 1.5 marks each.
• The scheme accepts other reasonable reasons.
hint: Think about its size and openness, and the number of connected devices.

body: Online shopping has been accepted as the easiest means of buying and selling, although there are risks. As an expert, suggest two ways by which fraud in online shopping can be minimized or prevented.
answer:
Any two:
• Use a different password for every account and add extra security with multi-factor authentication.
• Use automatic alerts to monitor your accounts.
• Avoid paying by credit card where possible and pay by debit card instead (as the scheme advises).
• Avoid public networks or public computers for digital transactions.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• 2 marks each for any two valid, explained suggestions.
hint: Think about passwords and authentication, alerts, how you pay, and which networks you use.

body: State two main benefits of using management information systems (MIS) in a company.
answer:
Any two:
• Real-time performance and analytical reports.
• Aids the work allocation process.
• Improves internal communication.
• Improves transaction processing.
• Supports decision making and enhances performance.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• 2 marks each for any two valid benefits, explained.
hint: Think of reports, allocating work, communication, transactions and decisions.

body: Differentiate between information and data.
answer: Data are raw, unprocessed facts that need context to become useful or have meaning. Information is data that has been processed, organized and interpreted to add meaning and value.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Data: raw, unprocessed facts — 1 mark.
• Information: processed, organized, meaningful data — 1 mark.
hint: One is raw; the other has been processed to have meaning.

body: What are the three main components of an information system?
answer:
Any three of:
• Hardware
• Software
• Database (data)
• Network (telecommunications)
(People and procedures are also commonly listed as IS components and may be credited.)
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• 1 mark each for any three of hardware, software, database, network.
• Accept people and procedures as valid components.
hint: The scheme lists the technology components: physical machines, programs, stored data and the links between them.

body: The two-way relationship between organizations and information technology is said to be mediated by many factors. Give three of these factors.
answer:
Any three of:
• Structure
• Politics
• Culture
• External environment
• Business processes
(Management decisions is also accepted.)
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• 1 mark each for any three valid mediating factors.
hint: Think of the organization's shape, power, beliefs, surroundings and ways of working.

body: Give any three major risks associated with management information systems.
answer:
Any three:
• Hardware and software failure
• Human error
• Spam
• Viruses and malicious attacks
• Natural disasters such as fires, cyclones or floods
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• 1 mark each for any three valid risks.
hint: Think of failures, people, unwanted messages, attacks and disasters.

body: The government has recently been talking about a digital economy. Considering the problems in Ghana, give any three challenges the government is likely to face with this digital economy.
answer:
Any three:
• Cost of educating and training end users in digital skills and literacy — users must be capable enough to patronise the programme.
• Taxing online businesses — goods may be exchanged physically so transactions may not show on the online platform to attract tax.
• Lack of infrastructure (connectivity, power, devices) to implement the programme and support its use.
• Cybersecurity issues — fraud, hacking and data breaches.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• 2 marks each for any three challenges, explained in the Ghanaian context.
hint: Think of skills, taxation, infrastructure and security.

body: State the main phases of the Systems Development Life Cycle (SDLC).
answer: The SDLC comprises seven phases: Planning → Analysis → Design → Development → Testing → Implementation → Maintenance.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Award 3 marks for the phases in order; deduct for missing phases.
• Accept equivalent models (e.g. systems analysis, systems design, programming, testing, conversion, production and maintenance).
hint: Seven phases, from deciding to build to keeping it running.

body: State two advantages and two disadvantages of using the Waterfall methodology for software development.
answer:
Advantages (any two):
• Clear, defined set of steps and goals.
• Well structured.
• No financial surprises — costs are estimated up front.
• Testing is made easy against clear requirements.
• The outcome is clear from the start.
• Transfers information well through documentation.

Disadvantages (any two):
• Longer delivery time.
• Changes are difficult once a phase is complete.
• Excludes the client/end user after requirements.
• Testing is delayed until after development.
• Lack of flexibility.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• 1.5 marks each for two advantages and two disadvantages.
hint: It is sequential: good for structure and predictability, bad for change and late feedback.

body: Explain the difference between onshore outsourcing and offshore outsourcing of a software project.
answer: Onshore (domestic) outsourcing hires a team of developers located in the same country as you for the software project. Offshore outsourcing hires a team of developers located in a different country.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Onshore: developers in the same country — 1.5 marks.
• Offshore: developers in a different country — 1.5 marks.
hint: It is about where the outsourced developers are located.

body: Give two disadvantages of offshore outsourcing of a software project.
answer:
Any two:
• Cultural and language barriers.
• Quality control issues.
• Security and intellectual property (IP) issues.
• Payroll and compliance issues.
(Time-zone differences and hidden costs of managing the vendor are also accepted.)
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• 1.5 marks each for any two valid disadvantages.
hint: Distance brings problems with communication, quality, security and paperwork.

body: In developing a software project, give two reasons why the user has to be involved at every stage.
answer:
Any two:
• Users help predict how things will go, so the project delivers the desired benefits and outcome.
• They give their perspective on the true added value of what is being implemented.
• Involvement builds a bridge (relationship) between the project team, the sponsor and the users — users who took part are less likely to reject the system.
explanation:
Marking guide (5 marks):
• 2.5 marks each for any two valid reasons, explained.
hint: What do users know that developers do not, and how does involvement affect acceptance?

body: In the Systems Development Life Cycle there is always a need for a feasibility study. Give two reasons why a feasibility study is important.
answer:
Any two:
• Identifies valid reasons to advance or veto a project idea.
• Improves the focus of the project team.
• Provides useful information for the next steps.
• Determines whether the proposed system is economically, technically and operationally feasible.
• Evaluates current and needed resources and technology.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• 1.5 marks each for any two valid reasons.
hint: It helps you decide whether to go ahead, and with what.

body: On a software development journey, one may trip over a number of obstacles that could hinder the final outcome. Give two of these obstacles.
answer:
Any two:
• Underestimating the task at hand.
• Integration issues.
• Communication breakdowns.
• Unrealistic or mismanaged timelines.
• Feature overload (scope creep).
• Lack of alignment between sponsor and user needs.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• 2 marks each for any two valid obstacles, briefly explained.
hint: Think of estimates, integration, communication, timelines, scope and stakeholder alignment.

body: In the Systems Development Life Cycle, which of the following is the best way to gather data: review of documentation, observation, questionnaire or interview? Give two reasons for your answer.
answer:
This is subjective: the student's arguments count. Example — interview is best because:
• It allows in-depth, two-way discussion, so the analyst can probe and clarify requirements immediately.
• It captures opinions, feelings and informal procedures that documents and questionnaires miss, and builds user involvement.

Other choices are acceptable with reasons, e.g. questionnaires reach many users cheaply and anonymously; observation shows how work is really done; document review gives accurate formal records at low cost.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• Subjective — the student's arguments count.
• 1 mark for a clear choice; 1 mark each for two valid reasons supporting it.
hint: There is no single right answer — pick one and argue for it with two strengths.

body: A simple user ID and password is not a secure method of authentication, since this single factor is extremely easy to compromise. Give any two password policies or strategies that must be put in place to ensure passwords are secure.
answer:
Any two:
• Strong passwords combining uppercase and lowercase letters, numbers and symbols, plus multi-factor authentication.
• Different passwords for different accounts.
• Regular expiry — e.g. passwords must be changed after a set period.
• Alerts (e.g. by WhatsApp or e-mail) whenever the password is used.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• 1.5 marks each for any two valid policies.
hint: Think of complexity, extra factors, reuse, expiry and alerts.

body: Another method an organization can use to increase security on its network is a firewall. Give two major roles a firewall can play.
answer:
• It secures the network from cyberattacks by controlling incoming and outgoing traffic.
• It protects vulnerable systems and private data in the network from unauthorized access — by hackers or insiders.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• 1.5 marks each for two valid roles.
hint: What does it stop, and what does it protect?

body: Give two major positive effects of social media on a firm's business.
answer:
Any two:
• Improves brand awareness and increases customer engagement and loyalty.
• It is cost-effective marketing.
• Expands the customer base and market.
• Increases annual profits.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• 1 mark each for any two valid effects.
hint: Think of brand, cost, customer reach and profit.

body: Give and explain any two negative effects of social media on our society today.
answer:
Any two, explained:
• Privacy concerns and data security risks — personal data is collected, shared and leaked.
• Spread of misinformation and fake news.
• Cyberbullying and online harassment.
• Superficial relationships and lack of deep connections.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• 1.5 marks each for any two effects with explanation.
hint: Think of privacy, false information, harassment and relationships.

body: If the government gave you the chance to give positive advice on the use of social media, what two pieces of advice would you give to ensure culturally acceptable behaviour?
answer:
Any two:
• Respect others' privacy — do not tag people in photos or places, or share their posts, without permission. If you see inappropriate behaviour, clearly ask for it to stop and keep a record of the request.
• Be courteous and polite, even when disagreeing. Be an "upstander": stand up for victims of bullying and report offenders to the appropriate authority.
• Avoid personal attacks, offensive language and cyberbullying.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• 2 marks each for any two well-explained pieces of advice.
hint: Think of respect for others' privacy and courtesy online.

body: With a sketch, describe the star topology and state one merit and one demerit of it.
answer:
The star pattern connects every computer to one central host, hub or switch, which handles the network tasks; all communication between computers goes through it. It suits businesses with large amounts of rapidly changing data (banks, airline reservations) and allows close control of data. If a computer other than the host fails, no other computer is affected, but if the host or its software goes down, the whole network is down.
Sketch: a central node with separate lines out to each computer.

Merits (any one): easy to install and wire; no disruption when connecting or removing devices; easy to detect faults and remove parts; security can be implemented at the hub/switch; easy to add new computers.
Demerits (any one): needs more cable than a bus; if the hub or concentrator fails, all attached nodes are disabled; more expensive than a bus because of the cost of the hub.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• Description of the star topology — 1 mark; sketch — 1 mark (the answer is typed, so accept a clear verbal description of the layout).
• One merit: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for its explanation.
• One demerit: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for its explanation.
hint: Everything connects to one central device. What happens when that device fails?

body: With a sketch, describe the bus topology and state one merit and one demerit of it.
answer:
The bus pattern connects all computers to the same communications line; communication goes both directions along the line, and computers communicate with each other without going through a server. Any one computer being down does not affect the others, but a large number of computers cannot be connected this way and it is hard to run one line over a whole building.
Sketch: one straight cable (backbone) with terminators at both ends and computers attached along it.

Merits (any one): easy to connect a computer or peripheral; needs less cable than a star; quick to set up, good for temporary networks; usually the cheapest to implement; failure of one node does not affect the bus.
Demerits (any one): the entire network shuts down if the main cable breaks; terminators are needed at both ends; hard to find the problem when the whole network fails; performance degrades as computers or traffic increase; low security — every computer sees all transmissions.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• Description of the bus topology — 1 mark; sketch — 1 mark (the answer is typed, so accept a clear verbal description of the layout).
• One merit: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for its explanation.
• One demerit: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for its explanation.
hint: Everything shares one cable. What happens if that cable breaks?

body: With a sketch, describe the ring topology and state one merit and one demerit of it.
answer:
The ring pattern connects computers and devices one to the other in a circle. There is no central host holding all the data, and communication flows in one direction around the ring. It suits situations where processing can be done on the local PC. Rings can be less efficient than stars because data passes through more points: from computer 1 to computer 4 it must pass through 2 and 3.
Sketch: computers placed around a circle, each linked to its two neighbours.

Merits (any one): data is transferred without a bottleneck; transmission is simple because packets travel one way; adding nodes has little impact on bandwidth.
Demerits (any one): packets must pass through every computer between sender and recipient, which is slower; if any node fails, the ring is broken and data cannot be transmitted; the ring is difficult to troubleshoot.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• Description of the ring topology — 1 mark; sketch — 1 mark (the answer is typed, so accept a clear verbal description of the layout).
• One merit: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for its explanation.
• One demerit: 1 mark for the point, 1 mark for its explanation.
hint: Computers form a closed loop and data travels one way around it.

body: State and explain any four information privacy principles that should govern how organizations collect, store, use and disclose personal information.
answer:
Any four of these principles (from the Information Privacy Principles):
• Manner and purpose of collection — personal information is collected only for a lawful purpose directly related to the collector's function, only when necessary, and never by unlawful or unfair means.
• Solicitation from the individual — the person is made aware of why the information is collected, whether the law requires it, and to whom it is usually disclosed.
• Relevance of collection — information collected is relevant, up to date and complete, and does not intrude unreasonably on personal affairs.
• Storage and security — records are protected by reasonable safeguards against loss, unauthorized access, use, modification or disclosure, and other misuse.
• Information about records kept — record-keepers let people find out what records they hold, their nature and purpose, and how to get access.
• Access — individuals are entitled to access records containing their personal information.
• Alteration — record-keepers correct records so they are accurate, relevant, up to date, complete and not misleading.
• Accuracy before use — information is checked for accuracy and completeness before it is used.
• Use only for relevant purposes, and limits on use — information obtained for one purpose is not used for another unless the person consents, it prevents a serious threat to life or health, the law requires it, or it is directly related.
• Limits on disclosure — information is not disclosed to others unless the person is aware or consents, it prevents a serious threat, or the law requires it.
explanation:
Marking guide (8 marks):
• 2 marks each for any four principles: 1 for naming, 1 for explaining.
• Accept equivalent formulations (e.g. purpose limitation, data minimisation, security, access and correction, consent for disclosure).
hint: Think of the life cycle of personal data: collection, telling the person, storage, access, correction, use and disclosure.

body: What is biometrics, and how is it used in information security? Give examples of the personal characteristics it uses.
answer:
Biometrics is technology that identifies and authenticates an individual based on personal (physical or behavioural) characteristics. It is used for physical access control, electronic access control and monitoring devices, and can be combined with passwords, PINs and cards for greater accuracy and security.

Examples of characteristics: fingerprints, face, retina, iris, speech (voice), handwriting/signature, hand geometry and wrist veins.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• Definition — identifies/authenticates by personal characteristics — 2 marks.
• Uses (access control, combined with passwords/PINs/cards) and examples — 2 marks.
hint: Identification by something you are.

body: Define computer forensics and describe the two categories of forensic tools.
answer:
Computer forensics is the identification, preservation, extraction and documentation of computer-based evidence.

Forensic tools fall into two categories:
• Evidence preservation and collection tools — preserve the integrity of data on evidentiary media and make unobtrusive copies of some or all of the original data, e.g. write-protection tools and disk imaging software.
• Analysis tools — help the examiner analyse vast amounts of data: recover deleted files, recover data not allocated to a file, perform string and pattern matching, identify files, and list or catalogue files.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• Definition — 2 marks.
• Evidence preservation and collection tools explained — 2 marks.
• Analysis tools explained — 2 marks.
hint: One category protects and copies evidence; the other helps examine it.

body: Distinguish between RAM and ROM.
answer:
• RAM (random access memory) — also called main, primary or internal memory; the computer's working storage, like a blackboard. It holds the data and instructions currently being processed, and its contents are temporary (volatile) — lost when power is off.
• ROM (read only memory) — also called firmware; its contents are installed by the manufacturer on the motherboard or components and can only be read, not altered. It holds permanent, non-volatile instructions (e.g. start-up instructions) that remain when the machine is off.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• RAM explained (working memory, temporary/volatile) — 2 marks.
• ROM explained (firmware, read-only, permanent/non-volatile) — 2 marks.
hint: One is temporary working storage; the other holds permanent, read-only instructions.

body: Distinguish between application software and system software.
answer:
• Application software — "end-user" software the user interacts with; programs designed to satisfy a user's needs (word processors, spreadsheets, accounting packages).
• System software — programs that start up the computer and coordinate all hardware components and application programs (e.g. the operating system). Without system software loaded into RAM, the hardware and application software are useless; it works "behind the scenes" and underlies application software.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• Application software explained with an example — 2 marks.
• System software explained with an example — 2 marks.
hint: One serves the user's tasks; the other runs the computer behind the scenes.

body: What is a computer program, and why is software essential to computer hardware?
answer: A computer program is a series of logical and sequential instructions that the computer follows to solve a given problem; programs are commonly called software. Without software, computer hardware cannot function — software makes the hardware 'intelligent'.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Definition (logical, sequential instructions to solve a problem) — 1 mark.
• Hardware cannot function without software — 1 mark.
hint: A series of instructions; without it the hardware cannot function.

body: Explain the terms bit and byte.
answer: A bit (binary digit) is the smallest unit of data on a binary computer — a single 0 or 1. A byte consists of eight bits; it is the smallest addressable unit of data and represents one character.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Bit: smallest unit of data (0 or 1) — 1 mark.
• Byte: eight bits, one character — 1 mark.
hint: The smallest unit, and a group of eight.

body: What is the system unit of a computer? Name the two main parts of the CPU.
answer:
The system unit (also called the box or main unit) is the case that holds the chassis, microprocessor, main memory, bus and ports.

The CPU — the "brain" of the computer — is made up of:
• the Arithmetic and Logic Unit (ALU), which performs calculations and comparisons, and
• the Control Unit (CU), which directs and coordinates the computer's operations.
explanation:
Marking guide (3 marks):
• System unit described — 1 mark.
• ALU — 1 mark.
• Control unit — 1 mark.
hint: The box that holds the 'brain', and the two units that make up the brain.

body: Explain the four stages of the information processing cycle, giving an example of a device for input and for storage.
answer:
• Input — capturing data and instructions (e.g. keyboard, mouse).
• Processing — manipulating the data according to instructions (CPU).
• Storage — keeping data for future use (e.g. hard disk, pen drive, diskette).
• Output — displaying or presenting the processed data as information (e.g. monitor, printer).
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• 1 mark for each stage correctly explained; device examples support the input and storage marks.
hint: Data goes in, gets worked on, is kept, and comes out.

body: What is a word processor? State four tasks that most word processing packages allow users to perform.
answer:
A word processor is a computer application for producing printable documents: composing, editing, formatting and printing letters, memos, brochures and so on.

Tasks most packages support (any four):
• Mail merge — customised letters from a form-letter template and an address database.
• Creating indexes of keywords and their page numbers.
• Creating tables of contents with section titles and page numbers.
• Creating tables of figures with captions and page numbers.
• Spell checking (against word lists).
• Grammar checking.
• A thesaurus for words with similar or opposite meanings.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• Definition — 2 marks.
• 1 mark each for any four tasks.
hint: Beyond typing and printing: think of mail merge, indexes, contents pages, spelling and grammar.

body: What is spreadsheet software? State four uses of spreadsheets and explain what a cell and a cell address are.
answer:
A spreadsheet is a rectangular table (grid) of information, often financial, arranged in columns (identified by letters, from A) and rows (identified by numbers, from 1).

Uses (any four): cash flow analysis, decision making, cost estimating, inventory management, financial reporting, entering students' grades, preparing transcripts, payroll slips and cheque preparation.

A cell is the intersection of a column and a row. Its cell address is the column letter followed by the row number — e.g. column C and row 5 form cell C5. Cells hold labels (text), values (numbers) or formulas, and numeric data can be turned into charts.
explanation:
Marking guide (6 marks):
• Definition — 1 mark.
• Four uses — 0.5 mark each (2 marks).
• Cell and cell address explained with an example — 2 marks.
• Types of cell content or charting — 1 mark.
hint: A grid of rows and columns; think of the business and school tasks it supports.

body: What is a website, and what is a home page?
answer: A website is a group of related web pages dealing with the same topic, published by the same person or organization — like a magazine with many articles. The home page is like the front cover: the main entry page that tells what is inside the site.
explanation:
Marking guide (2 marks):
• Website — 1 mark.
• Home page — 1 mark.
hint: Think of a magazine and its front cover.

body: Define business process reengineering (BPR) and outline the key steps involved in a BPR project.
answer:
BPR is a powerful form of organizational change in which business processes are analysed, simplified and redesigned. Pioneered by Hammer and Champy, it is "the fundamental rethinking and radical redesign of business processes to achieve dramatic improvements in critical contemporary measures of performance, such as cost, quality, service and speed" (Hammer and Champy, 1993).

Key steps:
1. Define the purpose and goal of the BPR project.
2. Define the scope of the project.
3. Identify the requirements/processes that must change or improve to meet clients' needs.
4. Assess the environment — competitors, prospective changes in technology, legislation or socio-economic factors.
5. Redesign the business processes and activities in light of the above.
6. Implement the redesigned processes.
7. Monitor the success or failure of the redesign against set benchmarks.
explanation:
Marking guide (8 marks):
• Definition (fundamental rethinking and radical redesign for dramatic improvement in cost, quality, service, speed) — 2 marks.
• Steps — 1 mark each for any six in a sensible order (6 marks).
hint: Hammer and Champy: fundamental rethinking and radical redesign. Then go from purpose and scope through to monitoring.

body: State two advantages and two drawbacks of business process reengineering.
answer:
Advantages (any two):
• Centres on customer needs and gives appropriate attention to the business.
• Provides cost advantages that strengthen competitive position.
• Encourages a long-term strategic view by asking radical questions about how things are done.
• Reduces organizational complexity by eliminating unnecessary activities.

Drawbacks (any two):
• Resistance to change from employees who see BPR as a threat to their jobs.
• Lack of detailed guidance for actual implementation.
• Change is very expensive.
• Strong reliance on, or commitment to, existing processes.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• 1 mark each for two advantages and two drawbacks.
hint: Customer focus and cost on one side; resistance and expense on the other.

body: Define information security and explain the three core principles of the CIA triad.
answer:
Security is the protection of data from accidental or deliberate threats that might cause unauthorised modification, disclosure or destruction; the protection of the information system from degradation or non-availability of services; and the protection of humans against injury and harm.

The CIA triad:
• Confidentiality — authorised restrictions on information access and disclosure, including protecting personal privacy and proprietary information. A loss of confidentiality is unauthorised disclosure, e.g. a hacker breaking into an organization's database.
• Integrity — guarding against improper modification or destruction of information, including non-repudiation and authenticity. A loss of integrity is unauthorised modification, e.g. an intruder changing records for personal gain.
• Availability — timely and reliable access to and use of information and systems. A loss of availability is disruption of access, e.g. a power outage with no backup power.
explanation:
Marking guide (8 marks):
• Definition of security — 2 marks.
• Confidentiality, integrity and availability — 2 marks each (meaning plus an example of a breach).
hint: C, I and A — keeping data secret, correct and accessible. For each, what does a breach look like?

body: Explain any four types of controls organizations use to secure their information systems.
answer:
Any four:
• Administrative (procedural) controls — approved written policies, procedures, standards and guidelines: security and password policies, segregation of duties (no one person can initiate and complete a critical task, e.g. requesting and approving a payment), job rotation, IT audits, training and awareness, staff screening.
• Logical controls — software and data used to monitor and control access: passwords, network intrusion detection, access control lists, constrained user interfaces.
• Physical controls — monitor and control the work environment and access to facilities: doors, locks, air-conditioning, smoke and fire alarms, fire suppression, CCTV, motion detectors, fencing, guards, badges and swipe cards, man-traps.
• Software controls — built into software to monitor use and prevent unauthorised access: input, processing and output controls.
• Backup and recovery procedures — regular backups stored offsite, restored when the working copy is lost.
• Data security controls — logical and physical measures ensuring data files are not accessed, changed or destroyed without authority.
• Authentication — verifying the identity of a user by password, PIN, biometrics or smart card; multi-factor authentication combines two or more.
explanation:
Marking guide (8 marks):
• 2 marks each for any four types of control, named and explained with examples.
hint: Policies, software-based access controls, physical barriers, controls built into software, backups, and authentication.

body: What is an information system? Explain the types of information systems and the level of management each serves.
answer:
An information system is a set of interrelated components that collect (or retrieve), process, store and distribute information to support decision making and control in an organization (Laudon & Laudon). It also helps managers and workers analyse problems, visualise complex subjects and create new products.

Types by level:
• Transaction processing system (TPS) — operational level. Records and processes the routine day-to-day transactions (e.g. sales, payroll); high volumes of structured input and output; supplies data for higher levels; often critical to survival.
• Office automation system (OAS) — all levels, mainly data workers. Word processing, spreadsheets, e-mail, scheduling, desktop publishing, document imaging.
• Knowledge work system (KWS) — knowledge level. Supports engineers, architects and scientists who create new knowledge (CAD/CAM, simulations); needs powerful workstations.
• Management information system (MIS) — middle (tactical) management. Summarises TPS data into routine and exception reports for structured decisions; mainly internal focus; limited analysis (e.g. an annual budgeting system).
• Decision support system (DSS) — middle management. Supports semi-structured and unstructured decisions using models, "what-if" analysis, and internal and external data.
• Executive support system (ESS/EIS) — strategic (senior) management. Non-routine decisions needing judgement; graphical digital dashboards; drill-down; access to external data such as stock prices and news.
explanation:
Marking guide (12 marks):
• Definition of an information system — 2 marks.
• Each of TPS, OAS, KWS, MIS, DSS and ESS correctly described with the management level it serves — about 1.5–2 marks each, up to 10 marks.
hint: Define IS, then go up the pyramid: TPS, OAS, KWS, MIS, DSS, ESS.

body: Explain the four methods of transaction processing.
answer:
• Online transaction processing — data is entered interactively (online) into the system.
• Batch processing — transactions are collected and processed together at regular intervals (hourly, daily, monthly), e.g. a monthly payroll run.
• Real-time processing — interactive, and the database is updated instantly as each transaction occurs, e.g. an airline reservation system.
• Hybrid processing — a combination of the above.
explanation:
Marking guide (4 marks):
• 1 mark each for the four methods, correctly explained (an example strengthens the answer).
hint: Interactive entry, grouped processing, instant updates, and a mix.

body: When is an information system said to have failed? Explain how design, data, cost and operations can each cause system failure.
answer:
An information system has failed when it does not perform as specified, is not operational at the specified time, cannot be used for its intended purpose, does not fit the organization's work processes, or costs more to operate than the benefits it brings.

Problem areas:
• Design — if the design fails to capture users' real needs, the system fails; e.g. a poor user interface leads users to enter wrong data (an error turning a credit note into an invoice).
• Data — "garbage in, garbage out": erroneous or inconsistent data produces bad information useless for decisions.
• Cost — a system must be economical to run; one that takes more resources than it brings in becomes a "white elephant".
• Operation — procedural and process problems: no timely reports, system down when needed, frequent breakdowns.
explanation:
Marking guide (9 marks):
• Conditions under which a system has failed — 1 mark (any two conditions).
• Design, data, cost and operations — 2 marks each, explained.
hint: First the symptoms of failure, then the four problem areas.

body: Explain any four criteria that can be used to measure the success of an information system.
answer:
Any four:
• Level of system use — a system used widely across the organization has been accepted; users abandon systems they deem poor. Measured through observation, interviews, questionnaires and surveys.
• User satisfaction — users are satisfied when the system is accurate, timely, easy to use and learn, and free of operational problems.
• Ratings of the IT department and staff — positive remarks and attitudes towards IT staff show the organization is satisfied with their services.
• Achievement of system objectives — a successful system meets the goals set for it at the planning phase.
• Financial benefits — increased sales, lower operating costs, controls against fraud and eliminated inefficiencies.
explanation:
Marking guide (8 marks):
• 2 marks each for any four criteria, explained.
hint: Think about usage, satisfaction, attitudes towards IT staff, objectives met and money.

body: Explain four factors that determine the success of an information system implementation.
answer:
• Role of users — involving users throughout development and implementation means their requirements are met, and users who took part feel ownership and do not reject the system.
• Degree of management support — top management controls power and resources; its backing shows commitment, helps resolve issues and motivates users and the implementation team.
• Level of complexity and risk — simple, structured projects succeed more often than large, complex ones; risk depends on project size, structure and the team's expertise.
• Quality of management of the implementation process — success depends on the team's experience and ability to manage the uncertainties of the project.
explanation:
Marking guide (8 marks):
• 2 marks each for the four factors, explained.
hint: Users, top management, project complexity and risk, and how well the project is managed.

body: What is a system? State its four basic components and explain any three characteristics of systems.
answer:
A system is a group of interacting, interrelated or interdependent elements (subsystems) forming a complex whole to achieve set objectives (e.g. health care, banking, information systems). Its four basic components are input, processing, output and feedback.

Characteristics (any three):
• Holism (synergy) — the whole is more than the sum of its parts; the system can only be explained as a whole.
• Hierarchy — systems are made of smaller subsystems and are themselves part of larger "supra" systems; complex systems are decomposed into hierarchical subsystems.
• Interdependence — parts cannot be altered without affecting other parts; a manager's decision in one unit affects other departments.
• Sub-optimality — subsystems should work towards the goals of the higher system; when they pursue their own objectives to its detriment, sub-optimality exists.
• Hard and soft properties — hard properties can be measured objectively (items produced per day); soft properties depend on values or taste (a person's suitability for a job).
explanation:
Marking guide (10 marks):
• Definition — 2 marks.
• Input, processing, output, feedback — 0.5 mark each (2 marks).
• Three characteristics — 2 marks each (6 marks).
hint: Interacting parts with a common goal. Then think of holism, hierarchy, interdependence, sub-optimality, and hard vs soft properties.

body: Explain the following systems concepts: system boundary, environment, open system, equifinality, decoupling, and shared (overlapping) subsystems.
answer:
• System boundary — the features that define the extent of a system and separate it from its environment. Easy to establish in physical systems; in organizations boundaries are set by management, unclear and dynamic.
• Environment — all elements outside the system, especially those whose changes affect the system or are changed by it: customers, competitors, suppliers, technology, government policy. Not all can be controlled, but organizations try to influence them (e.g. advertising).
• Open system — has many interfaces with its environment, taking in inputs and influences and returning outputs; healthy open systems use feedback to adjust and reach equilibrium.
• Equifinality — the same or similar results can be achieved by different methods or processes; there is no one way, so the business should select the most efficient.
• Decoupling — loosening the interconnection between tightly coupled subsystems so each can operate with some independence (e.g. holding raw-material stock so production does not depend on exact delivery timing).
• Shared and overlapping subsystems — a subsystem can belong to more than one system (e.g. central purchasing serving several departments, a shared computer facility); this is efficient but changes must consider every system that shares it.
explanation:
Marking guide (12 marks):
• 2 marks for each of the six concepts, correctly explained (an example strengthens the answer).
hint: Edges, surroundings, exchange with surroundings, many routes to one result, loosening links, and parts used by more than one system.
